cpd.reflection: The module changed how I see the SP. Previously I treated the SP mainly as a scenario prop. The module positions the SP as a trained educational partner whose feedback captures something faculty observation cannot: what it was like to be the patient. It also made clear that inconsistent SP portrayal is a validity threat in assessment, because if two students meet a differently portrayed "patient", the task is no longer the same. This connects directly to my interest in how clinical reasoning is made visible and assessed in OSCEs.

cpd.title: Hand hygiene for clinical healthcare workers
cpd.provider: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (NHHI)
units: HLTINF006 - Apply basic principles and practices of infection prevention and control
cpd.reflection: The content was familiar, but working through the moments in a structured way reminded me where my practice is most likely to slip under time pressure. The highest-risk moments are Moment 5, after touching a patient's surroundings, and the transition between procedure and patient contact in a busy ED or CCU, when I move between bed spaces or handle shared equipment. The module also made me consider that students copy what clinicians and educators actually do far more than what we tell them.

cpd.title: The Basics of Infection Prevention and Control
cpd.provider: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (NHHI)
units: HLTENN060 - Apply nursing practice in the paediatric care setting
cpd.reflection: The biggest value for me was framing IPC as a risk-assessment process. In ED, a patient's infectious status is often unknown at presentation, so applying standard precautions consistently and escalating early to transmission-based precautions matters more than waiting for a confirmed diagnosis. The PPE sequencing content was also a useful reminder. Removing PPE is where self-contamination is most likely, and it is a step students and busy clinicians commonly rush.

cpd.reflection: Summary of learning: The session presented the live online quiz as a hybrid between a take-home Moodle quiz and an invigilated test. Questions are shown on a timed PowerPoint during scheduled tutorial time, and students answer on their own devices in Moodle, which keeps auto-marking and instant feedback. Each question gets 45–60 seconds, navigation is forward-only with one attempt, a tutor supervises, and students may bring an A5 cheat sheet. The main control shifts from technical measures such as randomisation to human supervision plus external pacing, which reduces the chance of AI use and answer-sharing. The six design principles were: Calibrate time pressure so it constrains without punishing. Use a regular routine as the driver of engagement. Use cheat sheets strategically, because making one requires synthesis. Plan for EAL and accessibility needs. Defer releasing correct answers to protect students on extensions. Open with an ungraded practice quiz. The limitations were stated openly: the survey had only 53 respondents, the data were self-reported perceptions rather than performance, and the study covered a single institution over one trimester. Application to practice: This format is directly transferable to formative knowledge checks in the HLT54121 Diploma of Nursing delivered through Moodle, where take-home quizzes are exposed to GenAI misuse. I would begin with an ungraded practice run and allow extra time for students working in an additional language. Because the evidence base is small, I would evaluate the approach against actual results rather than student perceptions alone. The cheat-sheet principle also fits the way enrolled nurses are expected to use reference resources in practice.

I couldn't verify the article's author or content, and a CPD record shouldn't describe a piece I haven't read. The piece most likely relates to Dr Kam Kaur's work. She presented a HERDSA Assessment Quality SIG seminar on 17 June 2026 on inclusion and diversity within assessments through immersive learning. In related writing, she describes on-Country experiences as foundational rather than add-ons, introducing students to Country as teacher and moving them from passive recipients to active participants. Please confirm that matches what you read before using any of it. Application to practice (draft; edit to match the article): This reading has direct relevance to teaching at Marr Mooditj, an Aboriginal community-controlled RTO. It raises the question of how assessment in the Diploma of Nursing can recognise relational and Country-based knowing, rather than only adding Indigenous content to existing tasks.

cpd.title: Supervision meeting minutes (private)
units: CHCPRP003 - Reflect on and improve own professional practice
CHCCOM005 - Communicate and work in the health and community services
cpd.reflection: Participated in a research supervision meeting with my academic supervisor to review progress on my Master of Health Professional Education research project. The discussion focused on the development of a scoping review examining the operationalisation and measurement of integrative clinical reasoning in simulation-based education for pre-registration health professions learners. The meeting involved clarification of key research concepts including competency rating, operationalisation of constructs, and measurement of clinical reasoning within assessment frameworks. Progress on the development of the research methodology, preliminary search strategies, and inclusion criteria was reviewed. We also discussed strengthening methodological rigour through consultation with a university research librarian to refine search terminology and database strategies. Initial collaborative research infrastructure was established through Covidence and the Open Science Framework (OSF) to support systematic screening and transparent research documentation. This activity strengthened my research literacy, scholarly communication, and evidence-based educational practice, supporting ongoing professional development as a nurse educator and researcher.

cpd.title: The Paediatric Assessment Triangle
units: HLTENN060 - Apply nursing practice in the paediatric care setting
HLTENN037 - Perform clinical assessment and contribute to planning nursing care
HLTENN038 - Implement, monitor and evaluate nursing care
cpd.reflection: This activity strengthened my understanding of the Paediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) as a rapid assessment framework for identifying the severity of illness in children. It reinforced the importance of observing appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to quickly identify signs of deterioration. The learning supports my clinical reasoning and helps ensure that my knowledge of paediatric assessment remains current. It also informs my teaching within the Diploma of Nursing program by providing a clear framework that can be used in paediatric case studies, simulation activities, and discussions about recognising deterioration in children.
